table.brief: On-call rotation: Week (rowspan 2) / Role (primary/secondary) / Engineer / Phone / Escalation notes

understanding.purpose: Show who is on call each week, how to reach them, and what to do when an issue needs escalation.
understanding.reading: Readers find the current week, distinguish primary from secondary coverage, then follow the row to the engineer, phone number and escalation instructions. The week cells span both roles, so their height can absorb some wrapping.
groups: Week and Role establish the coverage period and priority; each week groups a primary and secondary row.
Engineer and Phone identify and contact the person assigned to each role.
Escalation notes give the follow-up instructions associated with each assignment.
keep_intact: Phone numbers should remain recognizable and preferably on one line for reliable dialing.
Engineer names and role labels should remain whole where possible.
Week numbers and date ranges should remain easy to associate with their two rows.
may_wrap: Escalation notes can wrap at word boundaries.
Week labels and date ranges can occupy separate lines within the merged cells.
Engineer names can wrap between words if needed.

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Refine r1A by giving notes another 20px. Keep week numbers, roles, name components and phone numbers intact while testing whether wider instructions improve row rhythm enough to justify the additional scrolling.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Use a narrower week column and moderately wider notes than r0B. This keeps role labels, surnames and phone numbers intact while limiting total width to 624px; dates may wrap more, but their merged cells can absorb it.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Give engineer names enough room for one line and notes more space than in r0B, while keeping the week column compact. This tests whether easier name scanning justifies cutting farther into the engineer column at the viewport edge.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Keep enough width for Week and its number together, preserve whole role labels and name components, and use a moderate notes width. This brings more of Phone into the initial viewport and reduces horizontal travel compared with r1A.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Test r1C with a wider notes column: retain single-line names and phone numbers while giving instructions more room. This explores whether the added width produces a calmer, shorter table despite more horizontal scrolling.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Give week labels and dates more room, keep names wrapped between words, and use a middle width for notes. This tests whether clearer date groupings justify a modest increase in scrolling and note wrapping.

bad.name: r3A
bad.note: Reduce the week column to 75px while retaining intact role labels, name components and phone numbers. This brings more of the phone column into the initial viewport and keeps the more comfortable notes width; check whether the date wrapping remains usable.
bad.why: The narrow week column separates each week number from its label and fragments the dates across up to five lines, weakening the primary row groups.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Try a narrower phone column to reduce scrolling while retaining the wider notes column. Phone numbers may wrap at natural breaks, so check whether they remain recognizable and easy to dial.
bad.why: The week labels are fragmented, and phone numbers wrap across lines, making contact details harder to scan and copy.

rationale: r2A keeps week labels together, roles on one line, and names in a consistent two-line rhythm. Its wider notes column limits row height without requiring the extra width that r2C gives to names. The phone numbers remain intact, though readers must scroll to see them in full and reach the escalation notes.

general: Give row identifiers enough width to preserve their grouping and make repeated rows easy to scan.
Keep contact details intact when readers need to identify or copy them quickly.
Judge horizontal scrolling against the readability gained across the whole table, including columns initially off screen.
specific: Two-line engineer names work well here because the paired role rows have enough height for them.
The long escalation notes benefit more from additional width than the engineer names do.
The merged week cells make fragmented dates particularly disruptive to the schedule's hierarchy.

tradeoffs: r2C makes full names easier to scan on one line, but adds horizontal scrolling and leaves less of the phone column visible initially. r3B gives dates more room, but its narrower notes column produces less even row heights.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative design estimates, not browser-tested breakpoints; wrapping can change abruptly with small width adjustments. A designer might reasonably prefer r2C if scanning full names is more important than limiting horizontal scroll.

critique.good: The entire table fits in the viewport, and the shaded week and role columns provide some grouping.
critique.problems: The table is extremely tall and difficult to scan. Broken role labels, names and notes obscure words, phone numbers occupy several lines, and the escalation header fragments. Large blank areas in the merged week cells weaken the connection between each week and its two assignments.
critique.cause: All five columns are squeezed into 359px. In particular, the 67px notes column leaves only 46px for text, while the 70px role and 83px engineer columns are narrower than their longest words. The 74px phone column cannot hold a number on one line.

critique.good: Role labels and names remain intact, phone numbers fit on one line, and the week, role and engineer columns are visible at first. The shorter table makes the weekly groups easier to follow than in r0A.
critique.problems: The viewport cuts through the phone column, so readers must scroll to use a number or read the notes. Notes still wrap into tall blocks, leaving substantial empty space in the other cells. Dates also wrap across several lines.
critique.cause: The first three columns use 301px, leaving only 59px of the viewport for the 153px phone column. The 150px notes column provides 129px of text width, which produces up to seven lines in a cell. The 90px week column cannot hold the longest date range on one line.

critique.good: The week labels and dates form clear groups, names and phone numbers fit on one line, and wider notes give the rows a more compact, balanced rhythm.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the engineer column and shows neither phone numbers nor notes. The 403px overflow makes readers travel a long way sideways to reach the instructions.
critique.cause: The 140px week, 99px role and 150px engineer columns together consume 389px. The 220px notes column reduces vertical wrapping but adds to the total width of 763px.

critique.good: Week numbers stay together, roles are easy to distinguish, and names wrap between words. The wider notes column produces the shortest rows of the three designs without mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Dates break across several lines, and the initial viewport cuts into the phone column; complete numbers and escalation instructions require scrolling. Names occupy two lines even where the row has substantial vertical space.
critique.cause: The 90px Week column leaves only 69px for text, the 112px Engineer column leaves 91px, and the first three columns already use 301px of the 360px viewport. The 220px notes column makes the table 675px wide.

critique.good: This is the narrowest table, and the role labels, name components and phone numbers remain intact. It requires 50px less horizontal scrolling than r1A.
critique.problems: Week numbers split from the word Week, weakening the most important row-group label. The table is much taller, with large areas of empty space beside short role and name entries. Phone numbers and notes still lie beyond the initial viewport.
critique.cause: At 80px, Week has only 59px of text space. The 180px notes column wraps instructions into up to five lines, increasing row heights, while the first three columns consume 291px.

critique.good: Engineer names remain on one line, roles are clear, and week numbers stay together. The merged week cells keep each pair of assignments visibly grouped.
critique.problems: The phone header is cut by the viewport edge and almost the entire contact column is off-screen. Wide, single-line names sit within tall rows driven by the notes, creating unused space; this is also the widest design.
critique.cause: The 150px Engineer column moves the start of Phone to 339px and adds 38px compared with r1A. The 200px notes column still produces five-line cells, so the extra name width does not reduce the overall height.

critique.good: The week and role columns establish the two-row groups clearly. Names wrap between words, phone numbers remain intact, and the 240px notes column keeps the table relatively compact vertically without splitting words.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the phone column, leaving the contact number incomplete and the escalation notes offscreen. The date ranges wrap into several fragments, making them slower to scan.
critique.cause: The first three columns consume 301px, leaving only 59px of the 153px phone column visible. The 90px week column leaves 69px for its text.

critique.good: It preserves whole role labels, name components and phone numbers, and reduces horizontal overflow by 45px compared with r2A.
critique.problems: The viewport still cuts through phone numbers. Rows are noticeably taller and less even, creating large stretches of empty space beside the short role and name entries. The date ranges remain fragmented.
critique.cause: Reducing notes to 200px forces more lines in the instructions, including a five-line cell; reducing the week column to 85px further constrains date wrapping.

critique.good: All engineer names fit on one line, while the wider notes column keeps row heights relatively consistent. Week and role groupings remain clear.
critique.problems: The added space for names does not reduce table height, and the initial viewport reveals almost none of the phone column. It also requires the most horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 150px engineer column consumes 38px more than in r2A, while the 240px notes column still determines row heights. The first three columns now occupy 339px.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1C.why: Weeks, roles and full engineer names scan clearly, but the phone column starts at the viewport edge, so contact details and notes require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Everything fits the viewport, but roles, names, headings and notes break within words. The resulting tall rows are difficult to scan.

ref_auto.why: Roles and names remain readable and phone numbers fit within the initial view, but the narrow week and phone columns create many short lines, while notes still require scrolling.

r3A.why: Roles and names read cleanly, and the rows are reasonably compact. Week labels wrap heavily, and phone numbers and notes extend beyond the viewport.

r1B.why: Roles and names are clear, but the week labels wrap over several lines and the tall rows leave substantial empty space. Phone numbers and notes require scrolling.

r2A.why: Week labels, roles and names form clear groups, with names wrapping naturally and rows staying reasonably compact. Phone numbers and notes require scrolling.

raw.unsure: The supplied view cuts off the right side of the wider layouts, so I cannot fully assess their phone and escalation-note columns or the total scrolling distance.

r1B.why: Roles and names remain readable, but week labels break into several lines and the phone numbers extend beyond the viewport. Tall rows leave considerable white space in the visible columns.

r2A.why: Week labels, roles and names scan clearly, with a compact row rhythm. Phone numbers and escalation notes require horizontal scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Everything fits within the viewport, but headers, roles, names and notes split inside words. The narrow notes column makes the table extremely tall and difficult to scan.

ref_auto.why: Roles and names read clearly and the phone column is visible, but dates and phone numbers wrap heavily. Escalation notes begin at the viewport edge and require scrolling.

r3A.why: Roles and names are readable and the rows are fairly compact, but week labels are more fragmented than in B, and phone numbers and notes extend beyond the viewport.

r1C.why: Names stay on one line and week labels remain legible, but the wide name column pushes almost all of the phone column and all notes beyond the viewport.

raw.unsure: The supplied image cuts off the right-hand portions of the scrolling layouts, so I cannot fully judge the wrapping and readability of their phone numbers and escalation notes.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
